tutorial_example_entry.lesson_core_move: Locate poles of a rational transfer function in the s-plane and interpret their real and imaginary coordinates as decay or growth rates and oscillation frequencies for system behavior.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Pole Locations in the $s$-Plane

image_slots.image_description: An $s$-plane diagram with real axis $\sigma$, imaginary axis $j\omega$, and 3 labeled sample poles: $-2$, $-1+j$, and $1-j$ to show sign conventions.

blocks.text: Start by identifying where poles sit on the transfer function $H(s)=\frac{N(s)}{D(s)}$. A pole is a root of the denominator, so each pole value is a candidate for an exponential mode in the natural response.
Use the base case first: for a pole at $p=-1$, the response contribution is $e^{-1\cdot t}=e^{-t}$, so the mode is a decaying nonoscillatory term.
Now label any pole as $p=\sigma+j\omega$ and read this coordinate split directly.
Apply the rule: if $\sigma<0$, the mode decays; if $\sigma=0$, it sustains; if $\sigma>0$, it grows. This is the stability language you will reuse at every pole-interpretation step.
The imaginary coordinate $\omega$ sets oscillation frequency in radians per second, and if $\omega=0$, there is no oscillation. If $\omega\neq0$, include a sinusoidal component.
Checklist for each pole: read $\sigma$ and $\omega$, classify $\sigma$ for decay/growth, use $|\omega|$ for oscillation rate, then map the pole location to the mode form.

image_slots.image_description: A single-pole $s$-plane diagram with the axes labeled $\sigma$ and $j\omega$, showing the pole at $-2+j1$ and nearby axis/grid labels for coordinate reading.

example_content.example_prompt: Read the pole at $-2+j1$ from the $s$-plane and identify the corresponding term in the natural response.

explanation_blocks.text: Cue: the plotted point is at $p=-2+j1$, so first read the coordinate form $p=\sigma+j\omega$ directly from the graph.
Extract the coordinates: $\sigma=-2$ and $\omega=1$. These are the real and imaginary parts of the pole location.
Write the associated natural-response factor using that pole.
Separate real and imaginary effects with Euler form.
Interpretation: $\sigma=-2$ gives a decaying envelope, and $\omega=1$ gives sustained oscillation at $1\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, so this mode is a decaying sinusoidal contribution.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Real Coordinate of a Pole

image_slots.image_description: A single-pole $s$-plane figure on the real axis showing the point at $-3$, with labeled $\sigma$ and $\omega$ axes and a note that $\omega=0$.

example_content.example_prompt: Interpret the pole at $-3$ on the $s$-plane and choose the correct response-type statement.

explanation_blocks.text: Cue: read the pole location from the plotted point, which is on the real axis at $p=-3$.
The real part is $\sigma=-3$ and the imaginary part is $\omega=0$.
Use the mode rule from the prior section: a pole $p=\sigma+j\omega$ maps to $e^{pt}=e^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}$.
Since $\sigma=-3<0$, this is a decaying envelope. With $\omega=0$, there is no oscillation, so the response is a decaying real exponential term.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Imaginary Coordinate of a Pole

image_slots.image_description: An $s$-plane image with a single plotted pole on the imaginary axis at $j2$, labeled axes $\sigma$ and $\omega$, and a short annotation showing oscillation rate.

example_content.example_prompt: Read the pole at $j2$ and identify the oscillation frequency and mode form.

explanation_blocks.text: Cue: read the plotted pole location, which is $p=j2$, meaning the pole lies on the imaginary axis.
Extract the coordinates from $p=\sigma+j\omega$: here $\sigma=0$ and $\omega=2$.
Use the same pole-mode rule from prior sections and write the associated factor.
Rewrite the complex exponential into sinusoidal components.

Interpretation: $\sigma=0$ gives a constant envelope (no decay or growth), and $\omega=2$ gives oscillation at $2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. If needed, $-j2$ would oscillate at the same rate with opposite direction of rotation.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Poles with Both Decay and Oscillation

image_slots.image_description: An $s$-plane diagram showing a pole at $-0.5+j3$ with labeled axes $\sigma$ and $\omega$, and a small annotation for decaying sinusoid frequency and envelope direction.

example_content.example_prompt: Interpret the pole $-0.5 + j3$ and summarize the natural response behavior.

explanation_blocks.text: Cue: read the pole location from the diagram. Here $p=-0.5+j3$, so both real and imaginary parts are nonzero.
Write the coordinates in $p=\sigma+j\omega$ form and extract $\sigma=-0.5$ and $\omega=3$.
Use the same rule from earlier sections: a pole $p$ contributes a factor $e^{pt}$ in the natural response.
Separate the real and imaginary parts to read envelope and oscillation.
Conclusion: $\sigma=-0.5<0$ gives a decaying envelope, and $\omega=3$ gives sustained oscillation at $3\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, so this is a damped oscillatory mode.

sections.section_title: Comparing Pole Locations for System Behavior

image_slots.image_description: An $s$-plane with three poles at $-4$, $-1+j4$, and $-1-j2$, clearly labeled with their coordinates and arrows showing decay rates and oscillation frequencies.

example_content.example_prompt: For poles at $-4$, $-1+j4$, and $-1-j2$, identify which pole governs the long-term behavior and why.

explanation_blocks.text: Cue: read the three poles from the diagram and list each as $p=\sigma+j\omega$. The points are $-4$, $-1+j4$, and $-1-j2$.
Convert each pole into coordinates: $-4\to(\sigma,\omega)=(-4,0)$, $-1+j4\to(-1,4)$, and $-1-j2\to(-1,-2)$.

Compare real parts to find the slowest-decay envelope. The real-part values are $-4$, $-1$, and $-1$, so the two poles with $\sigma=-1$ dominate long-term because they are closest to the imaginary axis.

Interpretation: $-4$ is transient and decays fastest, while $-1+j4$ and $-1-j2$ are the dominant terms with shared decay rate $e^{-t}$; among them, $\omega=4$ gives faster oscillation than $\omega=2$.
Final ranking: long-term magnitude is controlled by the $\sigma=-1$ pair, and oscillation speed ranking is $-1+j4$ (faster oscillation) over $-1-j2$ (slower oscillation).

question_entry.lesson_core_move: Locate poles of a rational transfer function in the s-plane and interpret their real and imaginary coordinates as decay or growth rates and oscillation frequencies for system behavior.

image_slots.image_description: A single-pole $s$-plane diagram with axes labeled $\sigma$ and $j\omega$, showing one marked pole at $-1+j3$ on a light coordinate grid.
A single-pole $s$-plane diagram with axes labeled $\sigma$ and $j\omega$, showing one marked pole at $1-j2$ on a light coordinate grid.

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram shows one pole in the $s$-plane. Which choice correctly reads the pole coordinates and the associated natural-response term?

choice_blocks.text: $p=1-j3$, so the mode is $e^{(1-j3)t}$; the response grows while oscillating at $3\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
$p=-3+j1$, so the mode is $e^{(-3+j1)t}$; the response decays while oscillating at $1\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
$p=-1+j3$, so the mode is $e^{(-1+j3)t}$; the response decays while oscillating at $3\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
$p=-1$, so the mode is $e^{-t}$; the response decays without oscillation.
$p=j3$, so the mode is $e^{j3t}$; the response oscillates without decay or growth.

questions.correct_answer: $p=-1+j3$, so the natural-response term is $e^{(-1+j3)t}$ and the mode decays while oscillating at $3\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the pole as $p=\sigma+j\omega$ with $\sigma=-1$ and $\omega=3$. The associated factor is $e^{(-1+j3)t}=e^{-t}(\cos 3t+j\sin 3t)$, so the negative real part gives decay and the imaginary part gives oscillation at $3\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram shows one pole in the $s$-plane. Which choice correctly reads the pole coordinates and the associated natural-response term?

choice_blocks.text: $p=-1+j2$, so the mode is $e^{(-1+j2)t}$; the response decays while oscillating at $2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
$p=1-j2$, so the mode is $e^{(1-j2)t}$; the response grows while oscillating at $2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
$p=2-j1$, so the mode is $e^{(2-j1)t}$; the response grows while oscillating at $1\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
$p=1$, so the mode is $e^t$; the response grows without oscillation.
$p=-j2$, so the mode is $e^{-j2t}$; the response oscillates without decay or growth.

questions.correct_answer: $p=1-j2$, so the natural-response term is $e^{(1-j2)t}$ and the mode grows while oscillating at $2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read the pole as $p=\sigma+j\omega$ with $\sigma=1$ and $\omega=-2$. The associated factor is $e^{(1-j2)t}=e^t(\cos 2t-j\sin 2t)$, so the positive real part gives growth and the imaginary coordinate gives oscillation at $2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Real Coordinate of a Pole

image_slots.image_description: A single-pole $s$-plane diagram with axes labeled $\sigma$ and $\omega$, showing one marked pole on the real axis at $-1$, with $\omega=0$ indicated and a left-half-plane decay annotation.
A single-pole $s$-plane diagram with axes labeled $\sigma$ and $\omega$, showing one marked pole on the real axis at $2$, with $\omega=0$ indicated and a right-half-plane growth annotation.

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram shows a single pole on the real axis of the $s$-plane. Which statement correctly interprets the real coordinate of the pole?

choice_blocks.text: $p=-1$, so the mode is $e^{-t}$; because $\sigma<0$, the response decays without oscillation.
$p=-1$, so the mode is $e^t$; the response grows without oscillation.
$p=-1$, so the mode is $e^{-t}$; the response oscillates at $1\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
$p=j1$, so the mode is $e^{jt}$; the response oscillates without decay or growth.
$p=0$, so the mode is $1$; the response is sustained.

questions.correct_answer: $p=-1$ has $\sigma=-1$ and $\omega=0$, so the mode is $e^{-t}$ and the response decays without oscillation.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A real-axis pole has $\omega=0$, so it does not introduce oscillation. Here $\sigma=-1<0$, and $e^{\sigma t}=e^{-t}$ decays as $t$ increases.

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram shows a single pole on the real axis of the $s$-plane. Which statement correctly interprets the real coordinate of the pole?

choice_blocks.text: $p=2$, so the mode is $e^{2t}$; because $\sigma>0$, the response grows without oscillation.
$p=2$, so the mode is $e^{-2t}$; the response decays without oscillation.
$p=-2$, so the mode is $e^{-2t}$; the response decays without oscillation.
$p=j2$, so the mode is $e^{j2t}$; the response oscillates without growth or decay.
$p=0$, so the mode is $1$; the response is sustained.

questions.correct_answer: $p=2$ has $\sigma=2$ and $\omega=0$, so the mode is $e^{2t}$ and the response grows without oscillation.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A real-axis pole has $\omega=0$, so it does not introduce oscillation. Here $\sigma=2>0$, and $e^{\sigma t}=e^{2t}$ grows as $t$ increases.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Imaginary Coordinate of a Pole

image_slots.image_description: An $s$-plane diagram with axes labeled $\sigma$ and $\omega$, a single pole marked at $j5$ on the positive imaginary axis, and a small label $p=j5$.
An $s$-plane diagram with axes labeled $\sigma$ and $\omega$, a single pole marked at $-j2$ on the negative imaginary axis, and a small label $p=-j2$.

prompt_blocks.text: The image shows a single pole at $p=j5$ on the imaginary axis. Which statement correctly interprets its imaginary coordinate?

choice_blocks.text: The pole gives sustained oscillation at $5\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, with complex mode $e^{j5t}$.
The pole gives no oscillation because $\sigma=0$, so the mode is $e^{0t}$.
The pole gives exponential decay at rate $5$, with mode $e^{-5t}$.
The pole gives sustained oscillation at $0\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ because its real coordinate is $0$.
The pole gives sustained oscillation with mode $e^{-j5t}$ because the sign of $\omega$ is always negative.

questions.correct_answer: The pole is $p=j5$, so $\sigma=0$ and $\omega=5$. It produces sustained oscillation at $5\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ with complex mode $e^{j5t}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Read $p=\sigma+j\omega$. For $p=j5$, the coordinates are $\sigma=0$ and $\omega=5$.
Since $\sigma=0$, there is no decay or growth. The imaginary coordinate gives oscillation at $5\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

prompt_blocks.text: The image shows a single pole at $p=-j2$ on the imaginary axis. Which statement correctly describes the oscillation?

choice_blocks.text: It is sustained oscillation at $2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, with complex mode $e^{-j2t}$.
It is sustained oscillation at $0\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ because the pole has real coordinate $0$.
It is exponential decay at rate $2$, with mode $e^{-2t}$.
It is exponential growth at rate $2$, with mode $e^{2t}$.
It has complex mode $e^{j2t}$ because the oscillation frequency magnitude is $2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

questions.correct_answer: The pole is $p=-j2$, so $\sigma=0$ and $\omega=-2$. It produces sustained oscillation with magnitude $|\omega|=2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ and complex mode $e^{-j2t}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $p=-j2$, compare with $p=\sigma+j\omega$ to get $\sigma=0$ and $\omega=-2$.

The zero real part means the envelope is constant. The imaginary coordinate gives an oscillation rate of $|\omega|=2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$; the negative sign gives the opposite rotation direction from $j2$.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Poles with Both Decay and Oscillation

image_slots.image_description: An $s$-plane diagram with horizontal axis labeled $\sigma$ and vertical axis labeled $\omega$, showing a single pole marked at $-1+j2$ in the upper-left half-plane, with light guide lines to $\sigma=-1$ and $\omega=2$.

An $s$-plane diagram with horizontal axis labeled $\sigma$ and vertical axis labeled $\omega$, showing a single pole marked at $-0.25-j4$ in the lower-left half-plane, with light guide lines to $\sigma=-0.25$ and $\omega=-4$.

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram shows a pole at $p=-1+j2$. Which interpretation matches this natural-response mode?

choice_blocks.text: A decaying oscillatory mode with envelope $e^{-t}$ and angular frequency $2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
A growing oscillatory mode with envelope $e^{t}$ and angular frequency $2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
A non-oscillatory decaying mode with time factor $e^{-t}$ only.
A pure oscillation with angular frequency $1\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ and no decay.
A decaying oscillatory mode with envelope $e^{-2t}$ and angular frequency $1\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

questions.correct_answer: A decaying oscillatory mode with envelope $e^{-t}$ and angular frequency $2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Write the pole as $p=\sigma+j\omega$ with $\sigma=-1$ and $\omega=2$. The negative real part gives decay, and the nonzero imaginary part gives oscillation at $|\omega|=2\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram shows a pole at $p=-0.25-j4$. Which mode description is correct?

choice_blocks.text: A growing oscillatory mode with envelope $e^{0.25t}$ and angular frequency $4\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
A decaying oscillatory mode with envelope $e^{-0.25t}$ and angular frequency $4\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
A decaying non-oscillatory mode with time factor $e^{-0.25t}$ only.
A decaying oscillatory mode with envelope $e^{-4t}$ and angular frequency $0.25\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
A pure sinusoid at angular frequency $4\,\mathrm{rad/s}$ because the pole is below the real axis.

questions.correct_answer: A decaying oscillatory mode with envelope $e^{-0.25t}$ and angular frequency $4\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $p=-0.25-j4$, the real coordinate is $\sigma=-0.25$, so the envelope decays as $e^{-0.25t}$. The imaginary coordinate has magnitude $|\omega|=4$, so the mode oscillates at $4\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

sections.section_title: Comparing Pole Locations for System Behavior

image_slots.image_description: An $s$-plane diagram with three pole markers at $-5$, $-2+j6$, and $-2-j1$, clearly labeled with coordinates. Include light arrows or labels indicating each pole's real part as decay rate and imaginary part as oscillation frequency.

An $s$-plane diagram with three pole markers at $1+j2$, $-2+j7$, and $-6$, clearly labeled with coordinates. Highlight that the rightmost pole has the largest real part, while $-2+j7$ has the largest imaginary magnitude.

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram shows poles at $-5$, $-2+j6$, and $-2-j1$. Which statement correctly identifies the long-term dominant behavior and the relative oscillation speeds?

choice_blocks.text: $-5$ dominates long-term because it is purely real, and the complex poles are only short-lived oscillations.
$-2+j6$ and $-2-j1$ dominate together because both have real part $-2$; among them, $-2+j6$ oscillates faster.
$-2-j1$ dominates by itself because its negative imaginary part makes it decay more slowly than $-2+j6$.
$-2+j6$ dominates by itself because it has the largest $|\omega|$, while $-5$ gives the slowest decay.
$-5$ and $-2-j1$ dominate together because their imaginary parts have smaller magnitude than the imaginary part of $-2+j6$.

questions.correct_answer: $-2+j6$ and $-2-j1$ dominate together because they share the largest real part $\sigma=-2$; $-2+j6$ has the faster oscillation because $|6|>|-1|$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Compare real parts first. The pole $-5$ has $\sigma=-5$, while the two complex poles have $\sigma=-2$, so the complex poles are closer to the imaginary axis and decay more slowly.
The imaginary part controls oscillation speed, so $|\omega|=6$ for $-2+j6$ is faster than $|\omega|=1$ for $-2-j1$.

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram shows poles at $1+j2$, $-2+j7$, and $-6$. Which statement gives the dominant long-term behavior?

choice_blocks.text: $-2+j7$ dominates because it has the largest $|\omega|$, so its oscillation is strongest long-term.
$-6$ dominates because $|\sigma|=6$ is the largest real-axis magnitude.
$1+j2$ dominates because it has the largest real part, giving a growing envelope; $-2+j7$ oscillates faster but decays.
$1+j2$ and $-2+j7$ dominate equally because both are complex poles.
$-2+j7$ dominates because stable poles should be ranked ahead of right-half-plane poles.

questions.correct_answer: $1+j2$ dominates because its real part $\sigma=1$ is greater than $-2$ and $-6$, so it grows instead of decaying.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Dominance is controlled first by the real part. The largest real part is $\sigma=1$ for $1+j2$, so that term grows like $e^t$ and eventually outweighs the decaying terms.
The pole $-2+j7$ has a larger oscillation frequency, but its envelope is $e^{-2t}$, so it does not dominate the long-term response.
